content: Apoptosis-inducing factor 1, mitochondrial (AIFM1), is a protein encoded by the AIFM1 gene located on the X chromosome in humans. This protein is found in both the mitochondria and the nucleus, where it plays a role in nuclear fragmentation during caspase-independent apoptosis. AIFM1 is initially synthesized as a precursor protein consisting of 613 amino acid residues. It contains a mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS) at its N-terminal and two nuclear localization sequences (NLS). Upon import into the mitochondria, the first 54 residues of the N-terminal are cleaved, resulting in the mature protein. This mature form integrates into the inner mitochondrial membrane. The protein incorporates a flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) cofactor and adopts a structure comprising three domains: the FAD-binding domain, the NAD-binding domain, and the C-terminal domain. The C-terminal domain is responsible for the pro-apoptotic activity of AIFM1, while the FAD-binding and NAD-binding domains exhibit the classical Rossmann fold topology, which is characteristic of flavoproteins and NAD(P)H-dependent reductases. Additionally, three alternative transcripts encoding different isoforms of AIFM1 have been identified. Two of these isoforms arise from alternative splicing, which affects the inclusion or exclusion of the C-terminal and reductase domains. A pseudogene related to AIFM1 has also been identified on chromosome 10. The AIFM1 gene encodes a flavoprotein that is critical for nuclear disassembly during apoptosis. In healthy cells, this protein resides in the mitochondrial intermembrane space. During apoptosis, AIFM1 is cleaved at residue 102 by calpains and/or cathepsins, producing a soluble, pro-apoptotic form. This form translocates to the nucleus, where it induces chromosomal condensation and fragmentation. Furthermore, AIFM1 promotes the release of pro-apoptotic proteins, such as cytochrome c and caspase-9, from the mitochondria. In addition to its role in apoptosis, AIFM1 contributes to redox metabolism through its reductase activity. Mutations in the AIFM1 gene are associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (Cowchock syndrome). At the cellular level, these mutations impair oxidative phosphorylation, leading to severe mitochondrial encephalomyopathy. Clinically, these mutations manifest as muscular atrophy, neuropathy, ataxia, psychomotor regression, hearing loss, and seizures. AIFM1 has been shown to interact with HSPA1A, a heat shock protein. This interaction is supported by the domain architecture of these proteins. Both eukaryotic and eubacterial AIFM1 proteins contain an additional domain known as AIF_C.
